hello! i’m danielle from the fraser basin council, i will be your narrator while we learn about wood smoke and clean burning practices. i will guide you through each module and learning activity in the online wood smoke education course. welcome to the online wood smoke education course
let’s start with a quick tour of the course and its features. tour of course features

throughout the course you will see buttons that look like this: they lead to extra bonus material. did you know? for a list of sources used to make this course and links to additional learning material, go to the resources tab in the upper right corner of the course. next to the menu tab is a notes tab that has a transcript with all of the verbal and written text in the course. tour of course features
let’s get started! start course start course start course start course start course start course
module 1: clean burning and wood smoke: why it matters (part 1)

people burn wood for many reasons: aroma, warmth, or ambience gathering and chopping wood no other heat source the low cost off grid/self sufficient living no knowledge of health effects wood is considered a carbon neutral heating fuel why do people burn wood?

wood stoves and residential wood heat appliances are a major contributor, but other sources of wood smoke in your community may include: commercial kitchens fireplaces, campfires, chimineas, and beach fires open burning controlled burns outdoor wood-fired boilers wildfires backyard burning other sources of wood smoke did you know? what is a chiminea?

other sources of wood smoke what is a chiminea? chiminea: “a freestanding front-loading fireplace or oven with a bulbous body and usually a vertical smoke vent or chimney.” chiminea disadvantages: low chimney stacks inefficient at burning wood smoke lingers close to the ground

other sources of wood smoke did you know? outdoor fireplaces and chimineas fall under the same rules as all other backyard burning. before burning, check with your local government to find out if they are permitted in your community and what the rules for use are.

wood smoke and poor air quality how does wood smoke impact air quality? wood smoke contains a high level of particulate matter, called pm2.5 particulate matter-laden wood smoke often stays low to the ground, where people live wood smoke can be a major contributor to smog effects are worsened in valleys where the smoke can settle when these areas have little to no wind, wood smoke can settle in an airshed for many days.

during an temperature inversion, warm air is sandwiched between a layer of cold air at the community level, and a layer of cold air above. the warm air acts as a barrier, trapping pollution at the community level. image courtesy of windows to the universe normally, the temperature of a community is warmer than the air above it. the air becomes cooler with higher altitude, allowing pollutants, such as wood smoke, escape image courtesy of windows to the universe temperature inversions happen when winds are calm and the temperature is cool. image courtesy of windows to the universe wood smoke and poor air quality

wood smoke affects your health and the health of your neighbours. let’s learn more about how wood smoke harms our health, and the different ways it can impact our health and the health of our communities. health impacts

pm2.5 is small enough to pass through our nose and mouth. when we breathe, we inhale the particulate matter, which is able to travel deep into our lungs into the alveoli, causing serious respiratory problems. what are alveoli burning wood releases fine particulate matter, known as pm2.5 which is categorized as a toxic substance under the environmental protection act. health canada describes pm2.5 as “all small particles found in air measuring equal to, or less than 2.5 μm in aerodynamic diameter.” grd-adrendal. available from :http://old.grida.no/graphicslib/detail/pm25-and-pm10-size_0cd fine particulate matter (pm2.5)
located in the lungs, alveoli are tiny air sacs where oxygen enters the bloodstream. what are alveoli?

short- and long-term exposure to pm2.5 in wood smoke can effect your physical health. health effects of short-term exposure: respiratory & eye irritation headaches, nausea, dizziness, & phlegm build-up susceptibility to respiratory infections & disease increased risk of heart disease & stroke shortness of breath difficulty exercising health effects of short-term exposure

health effects of long-term exposure long-term exposure: linked to heart problems, chronic bronchitis, development of asthma, reduction in lung function, and even premature death. smog: wood smoke can contribute to smog, linked to increased hospital admissions and premature death. carcinogens did you know?
health effects of long-term exposure what does carcinogenic mean? “a substance or agent causing cancer” - merriam-webster dictionary
health impacts of long-term exposure did you know? current and former smokers are more susceptible to the health effects of wood smoke exposure.

older adults often have chronic health conditions, exacerbated by exposure to pm2.5 more susceptible to lower heart rate variability caused by breathing in high levels of pm2.5 children spend more time outdoors more active their respiratory systems are still developing breathe in more air in proportion to their body size *link between childhood lower respiratory tract infections experiencing chronic lung disease in adulthood. people with heart or lung conditions asthma chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (copd) effects on vulnerable populations wood smoke can effect anyone’s health. vulnerable members of the community are more likely to be affected, including:

some folks experience psychological stress about their exposure to wood smoke, and the potential physical effects of that exposure. people may avoid regular activity and exercise including: walking, playing, and running outdoors wood smoke can effect someone’s ability to enjoy activities both inside their home and outdoors. wood smoke effects on quality of life & mental well-being not only does wood smoke exposure affect our physical health, it impacts our quality of life and mental well-being.

physical stress from exposure to wood smoke, can affect neurotransmission which can exacerbate some mental health disorders. what about mental health? what about mental health? wood smoke exposure may also impact our mental health. oxidative stress and inflammation associated with wood smoke exposure can affect anywhere in our body, including the brain.

when airborne, soot warms surrounding air by absorbing solar radiation. when wood is incompletely burned, it results in the release of black carbon (also known as soot) into the environment. fuel costs for transportation and chainsaw use are not carbon neutral. wood heat has environmental impacts, e.g., soot. what about climate change? wood heat is considered carbon neutral but…

module 2: clean burning and wood smoke & why it matters (part 2)

epa certified stoves “deliver more heat from each load of wood burned and reduce wood use by 30 percent.” - efficiency nova scotia whether you collect your own wood or buy it from a reputable seller, upgrading your wood stove can provide you with significant cost savings. new epa-certified wood stoves and pellet stoves are much more efficient at burning wood and are capable of heating a larger area than older non-epa certified appliances. energy efficiencies and cost savings upgrading an old, smoky wood stove to a new epa certified wood stove can provide benefits in energy efficiency and cost savings!

heating alternatives to wood stoves when looking for an appliance to heat your home, there are a number of alternatives to a wood stove, including: natural gas or propane heat pumps electric heat pellet stoves let’s look at each option in more detail!

propane may be an alternative in areas where natural gas is not available. in colder weather, propane tanks may have to be heated. natural gas where available, natural gas heat is an upgrade from an old wood stove. natural gas can be used to operate boilers, furnaces, or fireplaces. gas fireplaces are easier to clean and more efficient than wood burning fireplaces. natural gas and propane what is natural gas?

natural gas is a fossil fuel and energy source that, over millions of years, has been formed deep beneath the earth's surface. natural gas contains many different compounds, but the largest component is methane.- us energy information administration what is natural gas?

heat pumps heat pumps: are popular for residents in warmer canadian regions, such as vancouver island. air source heat pumps absorb heat from the outdoors in the winter and force hot air out in the summer.

electric heat is found in many forms including electric furnaces and baseboard heaters. electric baseboards are popular due to their low installation costs, and they do not require onsite combustion to create heat. electric heat

among the cleanest available wood-burning appliances(although still produce some smoke) efficient burn processed wood pellets to create heat do not require the same level of attention as wood stoves pellet stoves

module 3: firewood practices

in british columbia: harvesting firewood on crown land for personal use requires a natural resource permit and adherence to the rules outlined in that permit. only downed or dead wood can becut for firewood. remember: always check your local regulations before harvesting firewood! click the button below if you need to review bc’s regulations on harvesting firewood once wood is split: 4-6 months for softwoods to dry up to 1 year for hard woods to dry obtain next year’s wood this year to make sure your wood is dry enough for use. if you purchase your wood from a private supplier, find a reliable wood provider who is supplying wood legally. make sure to use a moisture meter to check that the wood is dry enough for use. whether you purchase or gather your firewood, it is very important to make sure you: source it properly obtain it far enough in advance sourcing firewood

moisture content and curing firewood 12-15% moisture is the goal for optimal burning! after splitting, use a moisture meter to check your wood’s moisture content. most municipal bylaws require below 25% moisture, but…

splitting wood wood length: use wood in a variety of lengths, ensuring it can easily fit in your wood stove aim for the wood to be 7.5 cm (3 inches) shorter than the firebox splitting wood split wood in advance and stacking it to improve drying time an ideal width is usually no more than 15 cm (6 inches) in diameter make sure it is the correct length for your wood stove… splitting wood

firewood storage and seasoning properly storing and seasoning your firewood will ensure you will have efficient, hot fires. it will reduce the amount of smoke and pm your wood stove releases. let’s look at some tips for optimal firewood stacking and storage options

optimal stacking stack your wood in alternate directions to allow for better circulation and reduction in moisture. stacking firewood away from your home is a good choice for fire safety, pest prevention, and better air circulation.

store the wood for at least 6 months the best way to know you are burning dry wood is to not burn it for at least 12 months storage options when storing your firewood, cover the top, but leave the sides exposed keep firewood 15 cm (6 inches) or more off the ground this will help protect the wood pile from moisture

module 4: clean burning practices

list of safe and legal items to burn in wood stoves clean, dry newsprint and cardboard may be used for fire starter dry properly seasoned untreated clean it is important to know what you can, and cannot burn in your wood stove. some examples include… firewood that is: what to burn

remember, not all fuel sources are appropriate for all wood heat appliances. follow the manufacturer’s instructions before choosing what to burn in your heating appliance, and always check your local bylaws before burning. in many communities, it is legal to burn the following in your wood heat appliance, but always check your local regulations: untreated, seasoned wood or wood products (cordwood, wood chips, & ends from cut lumber) wood pellets and other pelletized biomass fuels manufactured fire logs corn kernels and seed hulls paper and cardboard (only for starting fires) what is legal to burn

remember, burning garbage and other household items is not only bad for air quality and could damage your wood stove, but is against provincial regulations. what not to burn when using your wood stove, never burn: unseasoned wood painted or chemically treated wood wet, rotten, or mouldy wood ocean driftwood processed wood products with glue (plywood or particle board) household garbage demolition debris glossy or colour-inked magazines, boxes, & wrappers

as your fire burns, the amount of smoke coming out of your chimney should steadily decrease within 15-25 minutes of starting the fire, you should see heat waves rather than smoke coming from your chimney before lighting your fire have ample fire starter: newsprint dry, finely split kindling (2.5 cm or 1 inch diameter) begin to start a fire by opening the air inlet damper the damper needs to be 100 percent open when starting or re-stoking your fire you may need to open a door or window when starting the fire to create a positive draft going up your chimney to ensure a fire is both clean and safe, adequate combustion air is required. install your wood stove where adequate amounts of air enter the room (such as near a window). alternatively, ensure there is a combustion air supply to bring fresh outdoor air into the room. starting a clean fire

whether you choose top-down or bottom-up: add larger pieces of firewood as the kindling becomes charred never overfill the firebox this will increase the time needed to reach the proper combustion temperature bottom-up begin by crumbling newspaper on the bottom of the firebox place small pieces of kindling in row across the newspaper last, place slightly larger kindling across the pile in the opposite direction top-down begin by placing 3-4 medium sized pieces of split firewood in a row on the bottom of the firebox add small pieces of kindling in the opposite direction finish with knotted newspaper sheets on top your fire can be built from top-down or bottom-up: let’s explore both styles… building a fire

monitoring monitor your fire regularly, checking for signs of incomplete combustion such as blackened stove glass or chimney smoke. re-stoking when re-stoking the fire, make sure the damper is 100% open to allow new wood to catch fire. add 3 pieces at a time for optimal burning efficiency. do not close the damper entirely! the fire might not burn hot enough charring the fire should burn brightly with well charred firewood approx. 15-20 minutes after loading the firebox. dampening after establishing the fire, it can be gradually dampened, with the damper going from 100% open, to a minimum of 15% open. maintaining a clean fire once you have established your fire, you will need to maintain it.

it is important to make sure your wood stove is well maintained, cleaned, and in a safe location in your home. wood stove and chimney maintenance play an important role in the longevity, efficiency, and safety of your appliance, while keeping wood smoke to a minimum. stove and chimney maintenance

if you are regularly using your wood stove, you should clean the ashes from the firebox as least once per week. cooled ashes can disposed of in your garden, or contact your local government to find out where to dispose of your ashes. cleaning out ashes

burning anything other than seasoned wood, and newspaper to start your fires, can increase the build-up of creosote in wood stove pipe or chimney. creosote build up also puts you at risk of having a chimney fire! prevention of creosote buildup is essential to: maintain efficiency minimize smoke and particulate matter that deteriorate air quality preventing creosote build-up

have your chimney professionally inspected and cleaned at least once per year. annual cleaning will help you avoid hazards such as smoke problems, chimney fires, and carbon monoxide poisoning. important items to review during an inspection include: checking catalytic converters, fire bricks,and baffle plates replacing door gaskets and seals cleaning and inspecting the chimney and stove pipe glass door maintenance servicing fans if you burn regularly in your wood stove regularly, check your appliance every 2-4 weeks for any wear and tear or creosote build-up. chimney inspection and maintenance

keep an area of at least 1 metre cleared around your wood stove keep a fire extinguisher near your wood stove make sure to check your smoke alarm and carbon monoxide detectors regularly did you know? other safety tips

most pellet stoves need cleaning every four to six weeks, or after having burned about one ton of pellets. pellet stoves are more complex appliances than wood stoves, and require a range of ongoing maintenance. did you know?
some wood stoves are equipped with catalytic converters… if your wood stove has a catalytic converter, you will need to replace it every five to ten years. catalytic converters

module 5:rules, regulations, and air quality advisories

make sure to check with your local government to ensure you are in compliance with all local bylaws that relate wood burning and air quality. some examples include: permit requirement to install a wood heat appliance; requirement to only burn seasoned wood; non-certified wood heat appliance bans; burning restrictions during air quality advisories; and requirement that new buildings not use wood burning as sole heat source. many local governments (which include municipalities and regional districts) have passed bylaws related to wood heat appliance use, wood burning, and air quality. the content of such bylaws vary by local government. local government and bylaws

air quality advisories are issued when pollutant concentrations exceed or approach limits set by government, and when these conditions are expected to continue or worsen. these advisories provide information and include health advice for the public. advisories affect when sources of emissions must be reduced, including limits on the use of wood stoves. air quality advisories air quality advisory notices

want to know if there is an air quality advisory in your community? provincial governments release air quality advisory notices to the public. you can also check the air quality health index (aqhi) for your community online. air quality advisory notices

it is important to check local air quality levels before burning, using discretion during air quality advisories: if wood heat is your only heat source, try to limit its use during air advisories be considerate of your neighbors and be mindful of smoke levels air quality awareness

if you have an alternative heating source, you should not use your wood heat appliance when your community is experiencing an air quality advisory because… it contributes to pm2.5 pollution it effects the health of you and your neighbours it is banned under many local bylaws when not to burn

this is the conclusion of the wood smoke education course. we hope that you have increased your knowledge of wood stoves & wood smoke, and can now apply it when operating your own wood stove. summary of course learning modules

Why do people burn wood?

People burn wood for a variety of reasons, including:

•Enjoying the smell, warmth, or ambience of a wood heat

•Enjoying gathering and chopping wood for exercise or pastime

•Wood heat may be the only source of heat in thier home

•The low cost of wood heat

•Like to be independent from the grid or self sufficient

•Being unaware of the health effects of wood smoke and

•Because wood is considered a carbon neutral heating source

Other sources of wood smoke other than wood stoves

Because communities have multiple sources of wood smoke, it is important for everyone to be educated on the causes of wood smoke and be prepared to do their part to reduce wood smoke in their local airshed.

While wood stoves and other indoor residential wood heat appliances are a major contributor to wood smoke, other sources of wood smoke in your community may include:

•Commercial kitchens that use pizza or bagel ovens

•Indoor and outdoor fireplaces, campfires, chimineas, and beach fires

•Open burning (from land clearing and forestry) and controlled burns to prevent wildfires

•Outdoor wood-fired boilers

•Wildfires; and

•Backyard burning

Extra / Bonus content

What is a chiminea? Wikipedia defines a Chiminea or Chimenia as “a freestanding front-loading fireplace or oven with a bulbous body and usually a vertical smoke vent or chimney.” Chimineas have low chimney stacks and are inefficient at burning wood, causing them to produce smoke that lingers close to the ground, creating a greater impact in your neighbourhood.

Did you know?: Outdoor fireplaces and chimineas fall under the same rules as any other form of backyard burning. If you do use one of these outdoor heating sources, make sure to check with your local government to find out if they are permitted in your community and what the rules around use are.

Wood Smoke and Poor Air Quality 1

•Regardless of the source, all wood smoke negatively effects air quality but you may be asking yourself what it is about wood smoke that reduces air quality.

•Wood smoke contains a high level of particulate matter, called PM2.5 which we will discuss later in the section called Health Impacts.

•Particulate matter-laden wood smoke often stays in low lying areas. This keeps wood smoke close to homes, neighbourhoods, and the places where people work, play, and live.

•In some communities, wood smoke can even be a major contributor to smog. These effects can be exasperated because many of our communities are in valleys or low-lying areas near lakes and rivers which provide the wood smoke a place to settle. Combine these geographical locations with little to no wind and wood smoke can settle in our airsheds for many days.

Wood Smoke and Poor Air Quality 2

Temperature Inversions are frequent in many British Columbia communities during the winter season. They happen when winds are calm and the temperature is cool. Normally the temperature of a community is warmer than the air above it. The air then becomes cooler with higher altitude, allowing air pollutants, such as wood smoke, to rise above the community.

During a temperature inversion, the opposite is true: a layer of warm air is sandwiched between a layer of cold air below at the community-level and a layer of cold air above. This sandwiched layer of heat acts as a barrier, trapping pollution at the ground level in the community.

Prince George and the Fraser Valley are examples of places in BC that experience Temperature Inversions due to weather and local topography. The sides of valleys act like walls, trapping air and air pollution in the valley.

Health Effects

The number one reason that burning clean and reducing wood smoke are important issues are the effects that wood smoke has on your health and the health of your neighbours. Let’s learn more about what it is in wood smoke that harms our health and the different ways it can impact our health and the health of members of our communities.

Fine Particulate Matter (PM2.5)

Burning wood releases fine particulate matter, known as PM2.5 which is categorized as a toxic substance under the Environmental Protection Act.

Health Canada describes PM2.5 as “a general term for all small particles found in air measuring equal to or less than 2.5 μm in aerodynamic diameter. [PM2.5] It is a complex mixture whose constituents vary in size, shape, density, surface area, and chemical composition.”

According to Health Canada “wood smoke can be responsible for as much as 25% of the airborne particulate matter, 8% of the VOCs, and 7% of the CO in the air,” in communities where wood heat is common.

Bonus Material:

What are alveoli?

Located in the lungs, alveoli are tiny air sacs where oxygen enters the bloodstream.

Health Effects of Short-Term Exposure

Even if you are in good physical health, short-term and long-term exposure to fine particulate matter and other toxins in wood smoke can effect your physical health and the physical health of your family and neighbours:

Health effects of short-term exposure:

•Throat, nose, sinus, lung, and eye irritation

•Headaches, nausea, dizziness, and phlegm build-up

•Increased susceptibility to respiratory infections, asthmas attacks, acute bronchitis, and aggravation of lung disease.

•Increased risk of heart disease and stroke as well

•Shortness of breath and difficulty exercising

Health Effects of long-term exposure:

•Linked to heart problems, chronic bronchitis, the development of asthma, a reduction in lung function and even premature death.

•Wood smoke can contribute to smog. Smog has been linked to increased hospital admissions and premature death.

What does carcinogenic mean?

•Merriam-Webster Dictionary defines a carcinogen as “a substance or agent causing cancer”.

Did you know?

•Current and former smokers are less able to resist the health effects of wood smoke exposure.

Wood Smoke Effects on Vulnerable Populations

Wood smoke impacts on pre-existing conditions and vulnerable populations Although wood smoke can effect anyone’s health, vulnerable members of our communities are more likely to have their health impacted by exposure to wood smoke.

Some examples include:

•People with heart or lung conditions such as asthma and Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease (COPD).

•Children. Children tend to spend more time outdoors, are usually more active, and their respiratory systems are still developing. Children also breathe in more air in proportion to their body size. Exposure to wood smoke can reduce lung function in children.

•Wood smoke exposure can cause children to experience increased congestion and wheezing as well as shortness of breath, asthma, sleep disruptions, pneumonia, and inflamed respiratory tracts.

•Lower respiratory tract infections in childhood have been linked with experiencing chronic lung disease as an adult.

•Older adults often have chronic health conditions which can be exasperated from exposure to fine particulate matter.

•Breathing in higher levels of particulate matter may cause lower heart rate variability (or in other words, hearts have a reduced ability to respond to changes in activity levels and physical strain). Older adults are more susceptible to this.

Wood Smoke’s Effect on Quality of Life and Mental Well-Being

•Not only does wood smoke exposure effect our physical health but it impacts our quality of life and mental well-being.

•Wood smoke can effect the ability of people to enjoy activities both inside their home and outdoors in their neighbourhood or community.

•Wood smoke can stop you and your neighbours from regular activity and exercise. People may avoid walking, playing, and running outdoors.

• Smoky or smoggy skies can limit the everyday enjoyment in communities, make communities less beautiful, and effect the level of community pride felt by residents.

•A feeling of psychological stress amongst some members of the population is associated with knowing one is exposed to wood smoke and the potential physical effects of that exposure

Extra / Bonus content

What about Climate Change?

•Wood heat may be considered carbon neutral but the time to fuel costs from transporting wood and chainsaws is not carbon neutral. Wood smoke also has environmental impacts. Let’s look at soot from wood heat and its environmental impacts as an example.

•When organic matter, such as wood, is incompletely burned, it results in the release of black carbon (also known as soot) into the environment.

•Soot only stays in the atmosphere for a few days to a few weeks but the Canadian Council of Ministers of the Environment explains that even in this short time soot “is responsible for a significant portion of current global warming.”

•When airborne, soot directly warms surrounding air by absorbing solar radiation.

•Soot also reduces the reflection of solar radiation off of the surfaces of snow and ice. This speeds the melting process.

What about mental health?

•Many of the aspects of wood smoke exposure that impact our physical health may also impact out mental health.

•Oxidative stress and inflammation associated with wood smoke exposure can affect anywhere in our body, including the brain.

•Physical stress can affect neurotransmission which can exacerbate some mental health disorders.

•Chronic disease is a risk factor for mental health disorders and exposure is influenced by air pollution.

Energy efficiencies / cost savings

•Upgrading an old, smoky wood stove to a new EPA certified wood stove can provide benefits in energy efficiency and cost savings.

•New EPA-certified wood stoves and pellet stoves are much more efficient at burning wood and are capable of heating a larger area than older non-EPA certified appliances.

•Whether you collect your own firewood and want to save time, reduce firewood storage space, reduce physical effort from stacking and chopping wood and save fuel from travelling to collect wood or you buy your firewood from a reputable seller, upgrading to a new wood stove can provide you with significant savings.

•Efficiency Nova Scotia states EPA certified stoves “deliver more heat from each load of wood burned and reduce wood use by 30 percent.”.

Heating Alternatives to wood stoves

When looking for an appliance to heat your home or recreational property, there are a number of alternatives to a wood stove, including:

•Natural gas or propane

•Heat pumps

•Electric Heat, and

•Pellet stoves.

Let’s look at each option in more detail!

Natural Gas and Propane

Natural Gas:
In many parts of British Columbia, natural gas heat is an available upgrade from an old wood stove. Natural gas can be used to operate boilers, furnaces, or fireplaces. Gas fireplaces are easier to clean and more efficient than wood burning fireplaces.

Propane:
Propane can be used in many of the same ways as natural gas and may be an appropriate alternative in areas where natural gas is not available but please note that in colder climates, propane tanks may have to be heated.

Extra / Bonus content

What is natural gas?
Natural Resources Canada describes natural gas as “a naturally occurring hydrocarbon. Hydrocarbons are a class of organic compounds consisting of carbon and hydrogen and include crude oil, natural gas and coal.”

Are you interested in learning more about the benefits and challenges of heating with natural gas? Check out (NRCAN link)

Heat Pumps

Heat pumps are a popular option for residents in warmer regions such as Vancouver Island or the Lower Mainland.

The most popular type of heat pumps in Canada are air source heat pumps which absorb heat from the outdoors in the winter and forces hot air out of the home in the summer.

Another type of heat pump is the geothermal heat pump. It works by drawing heat from the ground.

Electric Heat

Electric Heat is found in many forms including electric furnaces and electric baseboard heaters.

Electric baseboards are a popular choice due to low installation costs, their ability to fit in tight spaces, and the control they give to heat a home room by room. They do not require onsite combustion to create heat.

Pellet Stoves

Wood pellet stoves are a popular choice in northern communities and a good substitute if you want to use a wood heat source while also reducing emissions. Pellet stoves are among the cleanest available wood-burning appliances and are efficient. They burn processed wood pellets to create heat and do not need the level of attention that wood stoves require to keep heating efficiently.

Module 2 - Firewood Practices

In this module, Firewood Practices, we’ll look at best practices for:
Sourcing firewood;
Firewood moisture levels;
Curing firewood; and
Storing and seasoning your firewood

Sourcing Firewood

•Whether you purchase or gather your own firewood, it is important to make sure you are sourcing it properly and far enough in advance.

•In British Columbia, anyone who wants to cut firewood on crown land for personal use must obtain a natural resource permit and follow the rules outlined in the permit. Only downed or dead wood can be cut for firewood.

•If you purchase your wood from a private supplier, check with your network to find a reliable wood seller who is supplying wood legally. If you are buying dried wood, make sure to use a moisture meter to check that the wood is dry for use.

•Once wood is split, it can take 4-6 months for softwoods to dry and up to a year for hard woods to dry. Harvest or buy next year’s wood this year to make sure your wood is dry enough for use next season.

Extra / Bonus content


What is a cord?
The cord is the standard unit of measurement for firewood. In metres a cord measures 1.2 x 1.2 x 2.4 meters for 3.62 cubic metres. This is equal to 4 x 4 x 8 feet, or 128 cubic feet.

Moisture Content and Curing Firewood

•After splitting your firewood, use a moisture meter to check the wood’s moisture content. 12-15% moisture is the goal for optimal burning.

•Most municipal bylaws require “below 25% moisture,” but even 15-20% moisture can cause excessive creosote buildup in the chimney.

•When bringing wood indoors, give it some time to dry from outdoor dampness or lower temperatures prior to burning.

Wood Length and Splitting Wood

Wood Length:

Make sure to cut your wood to the right length for use in your firebox. Use wood of a variety of lengths, ensuring it can easily fit in your wood stove. Aim for the wood being 7.5 centimetres or 3 inches shorter than the firebox.

Splitting Wood

•For best results and drying times, split wood in advance and stack it. This will increase its exposure to air and will improve the drying time.

•Cut wood to the correct length for your wood stove and split it to the proper width, usually no more than 15 centimeters or six inches in diameter.

Storage and Seasoning Firewood

•Properly storing and seasoning your firewood will ensure you will have efficient, hot fires and will reduce creosote build-up. Most importantly it will reduce the amount of smoke and particulate matter your wood stove releases, helping to keep your local airshed healthy for everyone.

•Let’s look at some tips for optimal firewood stacking and storage options to help with the seasoning of your firewood.

Optimal Stacking

•Stack your wood in alternate directions to allow better circulation and a further reduction in moisture content.

•Stacking firewood away from your home is a good choice for fire safety, pest prevention, and better air circulation.

Storage Options

•When storing your firewood, cover the top, but leave the sides exposed

•Build a wood shed or structure to keep firewood 15 centimetres/ 6 inches or more off the ground. This will help protect the bottom of the wood pile from moisture.

•Cover the top of your wood stack, but leave the sides exposed.

•You can use a tarp to cover the top of a woodpile. When using a tarp be careful not to have the tarp hang over the sides so moisture is trapped.

•In warm summer months, you might want to remove the tarp to speed up the drying process.

•Store the wood for at least 6 months but the best way to know you are burning dry wood is to not burn it for at least 12 months.

Module 3 – Clean Burning Practices

What to Burn

Before starting your fire in your wood stove, it is important to review what can and cannot be burned in your wood stove appliance.

Some examples of what can legally and safely be burned in your wood stove include:

•Untreated, clean, dry, properly seasoned firewood

•Also, Clean, dry newsprint and cardboard may be used for starting your fire.

Extra / Bonus content
Looking for other items you can legally and safely burn in your wood stove?

In British Columbia, it is legal to use the following fuel sources in your wood heating appliance

1) Untreated, seasoned wood or wood products. This includes cordwood, wood chips, and ends from cutting lumber to length

2) Wood pellets and other pelletized biomass fuels

3) Manufactured fire logs

4) Corn kernels and seed hulls

5) Paper and cardboard only for starting fires

Remember, not all fuel sources are appropriate for all wood heat appliances. Follow the manufacturer’s instructions before choosing what to burn in your heating appliance.

What Not to Burn

When using your wood stove, never burn:

•Unseasoned wood

•Wood that has been painted or chemically treated

•Wood that is wet, has signs of rot or disease, moldy wood, or ocean driftwood

•Any processed wood products with glue (e.g., plywood or particle board)

•Household garbage or cardboard, including plastics, foam, and rubber

•Demolition debris or other rubbers

•Glossy or colour-inked magazines, boxes, or wrappers

Remember, burning garbage and other household items is not only bad for air quality and could damage your wood stove but is against provincial regulations. More detailed information is available in Module 4 - Rules, Regulations and Advisories

Starting a Clean Fire

Let’s look at how to start a clean fire, including the role of air flow, how to operate the damper, combustion air, and fire-starting materials.

•To ensure a fire is both clean and safe, adequate combustion air is required. Locate your wood stove where adequate amounts of air enter the room, such as in proximity to a window. Alternatively, ensure there is a combustion air supply to bring fresh outdoor air into the room.

•When starting a fire in your stove, begin with opening the air inlet damper. The damper needs to be 100 percent open when starting or re-stoking your fire. Sometimes you may need to open a door or window when starting your fire to create a positive draft going up your chimney.

•Before lighting your fire, ensure that you have ample newsprint and dry, finely split kindling to use as fire starter that is 2.5 centimeters or 1 inch in diameter

•As your fire burns, the amount of smoke you can see coming out of the chimney should steadily decrease. Within 15-25 minutes of starting your fire, you should see heat waves rather than smoke coming from your chimney.

Starting a Fire

Top-Down and Bottom-Up Techniques

When starting your fire, it can be built from top-down or bottom-up. Let’s explore both styles.

Top-Down Technique
To start a fire top-down, begin by placing 3-4 medium sized pieces of split firewood (7.5 - 10 centimeters/3-4 inches in diameter) in a row on the bottom of the firebox.

•Add small pieces of kindling (2.5 centimeters/1 inch diameter) across in the opposite direction.

•Top this off with knotted newspaper sheets on top (roll the newspaper in a tube and tie it into a knot).

Bottom-Up Technique
To start a fire bottom-up, begin by crumbling newspaper on the bottom of the firebox.

•Place small pieces of kindling in rows across the newspaper. Then place slightly larger kindling

•across the small kindling in the opposite direction.

•Whether you choose the top-down or bottom-up method:

•Larger pieces of firewood (7.5-15 centimeters or 3-6 inches in diameter) can be added as the kindling becomes charred.

•Never overfill the firebox. Overfilling the firebox will increase the time needed to reach the proper combustion temperature in your wood stove appliance.

Maintaining a Clean Fire

•Once you have established your fire, you will need to maintain it, keeping the following information in mind:

•Charring: The fire should burn brightly with well charred firewood approximately 15-20 minutes after loading the firebox with larger pieces of wood.

•Dampening the fire: after establishing the fire, it can be gradually dampened, with the damper going from 100 percent open to a minimum of 15 percent open. Do not close the damper entirely as your fire may be at risk of not being hot enough for the secondary burn.

•Monitoring the fire: Ensure you monitor your fire regularly, checking for signs of incomplete combustion such as blackened stove glass, lay flames, or chimney smoke.

•Re-stoking the fire: When re-stoking the fire, make sure the damper is 100 percent open for 15-20 minutes to allow the additional wood to catch fire. Add 3 pieces of firewood at a time for optimal burning efficiency.

Introduction to Stove and Chimney Maintenance

•There is so much to learn when it comes to the maintenance of your wood stove and chimney. This section will provide an introduction to these topics.

•Safety is always a top priority when using any heating appliances in our homes. It is important to make sure your wood stove is well maintained, cleaned, and is in a safe location in your home.

•Wood stove and chimney maintenance plays an important role in the longevity, efficiency, and safety of you appliance while also keeping wood smoke to a minimum.

•Let’s review some key safety issues to keep in mind when using your wood stove, including cleaning out ashes, burning dry wood, chimney inspection and maintenance, and preventing creosote build-up.

Cleaning Out Ashes

if you are regularly using your wood stove, you should clean the ashes from the firebox as least once per week. Store the ashes in a metal container until they are cool to the touch. Once cooled, they can be disposed of in your garden or through your local government’s waste disposal services. Many local governments have restrictions on wood ash. Make sure to contact your local government to find out where to dispose of your ashes.

Preventing Creosote Build-Up

•Prevention of creosote buildup is essential to maintaining optimal efficiency, minimal smoke, and a reduction in particulate matter emissions for indoor and outdoor air quality. Creosote build up also puts you at risk of having a chimney fire.

•Burning anything other than seasoned wood and newspaper to start your fires can increase the build-up of creosote in the wood stove pipe or chimney.

Chimney Inspection and Maintenance

•Your chimney should be inspected and cleaned regularly to prevent creosote build-up.

•If you burn in your wood stove regularly, check your appliance every 2-4 weeks for any wear and tear.

•Have your chimney professionally inspected and cleaned at least once per year. Look for a chimney sweep or wood heating retailer certified by the Wood Energy Technical Training (WETT) program. A WETT certified chimney sweep will look at your wood heating system from the top of the chimney downwards and might suggest to you when you should replace wood stove parts. Annual cleaning will help you avoid hazards such as smoking problems, chimney fires, and carbon monoxide poisoning.

Important items to review during an inspection include:

•Checking catalytic converters, fire bricks, and baffle plates;

•Replacing door gaskets and seals;

•Cleaning and inspecting the chimney and stove pipe;

•Glass door maintenances; and

•Servicing fans

Other Safety Tips

•Let’s look at some other safety tips related to using your wood stove and chimney. Ensure you have an area of at least one metre/ 3 and a half feet cleared around your wood stove to prevent anything from catching fire.

•Keep a fire extinguisher near your wood stove in case there is a fire.

•Make sure to check your smoke alarm and carbon monoxide detectors regularly.

Wood Stoves With Catalytic Converters

Some wood stoves are equipped with catalytic converters. If your wood stove has a catalytic converter, you will need to replace it every five to ten years.

Extra / Bonus content

What is a catalytic converter and what does it do?: These converters are ceramic combustors coated with palladium. The catalytic converter is located in the wood stove downstream of the firebox. The catalyst reduces the ignition temperature of the smoke so it burns more completely, reducing smoke emissions at normal stove operating temperatures

Module 4 - Rules,Regulations and Air Quality Advisories

In Module 4 – our last module - we will review rules and regulations around wood smoke and wood heating appliance use as well as some basic information around air quality advisories.

Rules and regulations: Why are they in place?

Whether at the Provincial level or local government level (examples: cities, regional districts), there are a variety of rules and regulations that have to be followed for using wood stoves. Let’s explore some examples of the rules and regulations you will want to familiarize yourself with related to using your wood burning appliance, including:

•The Open Burning Smoke Control Regulations;

•Solid Fuel Burning Domestic Appliance Regulation;

•General information on local government and bylaws;

•Metro Vancouver and air quality regulation;

•Air quality advisories; and

•When not to burn.

Local Government and Bylaws

Many local governments, which include municipalities and regional districts, have passed bylaws related to wood heat appliance use, wood burning, and air quality.

The content of such bylaws vary by local government but some examples found in British Columbia include:

•A requirement to have a permit to install a wood heat appliance;

•A requirement for installations to comply with building code;

•Requirements to only burn seasoned wood;

•Limits on the type of wood heat appliance installed;

•A ban on non-certified wood heat appliances;

•A ban on outdoor solid burning appliances such as outdoor wood heat boilers;

•Wood burning restrictions during air quality advisories; and

•A requirements for new buildings to not use wood stoves as sole source of heat.

Make sure to contact your local government to ensure you are in compliance with all of the local bylaws that relate to wood burning and air quality.

Air Quality Advisories

Now we will learn more about air quality advisories. Local monitoring stations in communities throughout British Columbia collect information on air quality, including levels of PM2.5

•Air quality advisories are issued when concentrations of pollutants exceed or approach limits set by government. Air quality advisories are also issued when poor air quality is expected to continue or worsen.

•These advisories help provide information so residents can make choices about reducing their exposure to poor air quality days and include health advice for the public.

•Advisories take affect when sources of emissions must be reduced, including putting limits on the use of wood stoves.

Extra / Bonus content

Want to know if there is an air quality advisory in your community? The BC Ministry of Environment and Climate Change Strategy releases air quality advisory notices to the public. You can also check the air quality health index (AQHI) for your community on an interactive map found on the Ministry’s website.

Air Quality Awareness

•It is important for every wood heat appliance owner to be proactive in checking local air quality levels before using their appliances.

•When air quality advisories are issued, please use discretion when burning. You cannot use wood heat during an air quality advisory if you have a secondary source of heat. If wood heat is your only heat source, try to limit its use during air advisories by dressing warm and ensuring your home is well insulated. As always, it is important to run your wood stove hot enough so that it can burn clean and won’t add unnecessary smoke to the local airshed.

•Be considerate of your neighbors while burning wood and be mindful of smoke levels even when there are no air quality advisories in place. And remember, seniors, children, and those with respiratory and cardiovascular diseases are more susceptible to particulate matter in the air.

When Not To Burn

If you have an alternative heating source to burning wood, you should not use your wood stove or other wood heat appliance when you community is experiencing air quality advisory days as it contributes to particulate matter, effects the health of you and your neighbours and in many communities is banned under local bylaws.
